Everything else is explanation.\n29\t\n30\t---\n31\t\n32\t## 1. Objective\n33\t\n34\t> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n35\t> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n36\t> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n37\t>\n38\t> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n39\t\n40\t- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n41\t  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n42\t- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n43\t- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n44\t- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n45\t\n46\t### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n47\t\n48\tMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\n49\tdesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\n50\tBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n51\t\n52\t| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n53\t|---|---|---|---|\n54\t| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n55\t| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n56\t| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n57\t| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n58\t| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n59\t\n60\t> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n61\t> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n62\t> one would overstate throughput.\n63\t\n64\t**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\n65\tand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n66\t\n67\t1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n68\t2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n69\t3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n70\t   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n71\t\n72\t---\n73\t\n74\t## 2. Glossary\n75\t\n76\tSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n77\t(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\n78\tplan they mean exactly this:\n79\t\n80\t| Term | Meaning here |\n81\t|---|---|\n82\t| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n83\t| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n84\t| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n85\t| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n86\t| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n87\t| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n88\t| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n89\t| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n90\t| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n91\t| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n92\t| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n93\t| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n94\t| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n95\t| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n96\t| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n97\t| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n98\t| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n99\t\n100\t---\n101\t\n102\t## 3. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n103\t\n104\tFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n105\t\n106\t### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n107\t\n108\tThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\n109\tversion of this section got it half right.\n110\t\n111\tD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n112\t[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\n113\tThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\n114\tblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n115\t\n116\t**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n117\t\n118\tEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\n119\toperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\n120\tfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\n121\tand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n122\t**sustain**:\n123\t\n124\t```\n125\trequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n126\t```\n127\t\n128\t> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n129\t> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n130\t> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n131\t> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n132\t\n133\tAll figures below are emitted by\n134\t[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\n135\tmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\n136\tare comparable:\n137\t\n138\t| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n139\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n140\t| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n141\t| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n142\t| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n143\t| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n144\t\n145\tThe plan's own evidence base\n146\t([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\n147\tstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\n148\tthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\n149\tabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n150\t\n151\tIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\n152\tmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\n153\tgot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n154\t\n155\t**Two further findings from the model:**\n156\t\n157\t- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. Everything else is explanation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Objective\n\n> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n>\n> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n\n- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n\n### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n\nMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\ndesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\nBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n\n| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n\n> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n> one would overstate throughput.\n\n**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\nand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n\n1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Glossary\n\nSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\nplan they mean exactly this:\n\n| Term | Meaning here |\n|---|---|\n| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n\n---\n\n## 3. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n\nFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n\n### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n\nThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\nversion of this section got it half right.\n\nD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\nThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\nblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n\n**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n\nEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\noperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\nfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\nand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n**sustain**:\n\n```\nrequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n```\n\n> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n\nAll figures below are emitted by\n[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\nmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\nare comparable:\n\n| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n\nThe plan's own evidence base\n([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\nstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\nthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\nabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n\nIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\nmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\ngot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n\n**Two further findings from the model:**\n\n- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. So K MUST\n  be sized for the *fastest* stage we intend to reach (Stage 3, 106 KB/s), not the\n  slowest. This is counterintuitive and is why the original error was easy to make.\n- **The sender's cost was unbudgeted too.** §6.3.1 counted QR encode and render but not\n  the fountain XOR. At uncapped harmonic degree and K = 16,384 that is 398 KB of XOR\n  per packet — **91.8 MB/s** at the old 225 packets/s (1 packet/tile), or **183.6 MB/s**\n  at the adopted 450 packets/s (2 packets/tile at R2 nominal), on top of everything\n  else. Hence D25.\n\n**Fix — D19:** K = **768**, L = **256 B**, block = **192.0 KB**.\n\n| | Was | Now |\n|---|---|---|\n| K | 16,384 | **768** |\n| L | 256 B | **256 B** (unchanged — see §3.1.1) |\n| Block | 4 MB | **192.0 KB** |\n| GE matrix | 32.0 MB | **72.0 KB** |\n| Block-layer working set | ~36 MB (claimed) | **264.0 KB** |\n| Sustained need @ Stage 3 | 14.9 GB/s | **114.6 MB/s** |\n\n*Both \"sustained need\" figures are at Stage 3, so they compare like with like. The\n4.5 GB/s in the table above is the same design at Stage 1.*\n\n**K_max at Stage 3 is 1152.** We adopt **768** deliberately below the ceiling —\nD26 requires the sender to assume the weaker receiver, and the 200 MB/s budget has\nbeen measured (S1: 3,260 MB/s desktop). At 15 fps, this geometry delivers **7.5 KB × 15 fps = 112.5 KB/s payload rate** (or ~113 KB/s) before fountain overhead and erasure loss.\n431\t\n432\t**Why 15 tiles when the table shows 8?** The table above shows the tile count that fits when targeting exactly 4 camera px/module. Each packet is 269 B (13-byte header + 256 B payload), so 2 packets = 538 B per tile, which fits within v16-L's 586 B capacity. The **user-visible payload** is 15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 256 B = **7,680 B/frame ≈ 7.5 KB/frame**. The **8.6 KB/frame QR capacity** is 15 tiles × 586 B (v16-L capacity) = 8,790 B. At 15 fps, this geometry delivers **7.5 KB × 15 fps = 112.5 KB/s payload rate** (or ~113 KB/s) before fountain overhead and erasure loss.\n\n**Why 15 tiles when the table shows 8?** The table above shows the tile count that fits when targeting exactly 4 camera px/module. The actual design uses 15 tiles at ~1-2 screen px/module, which achieves ~2-2.5 camera px/module (below the 4.0 cliff threshold but still functional based on S3 measurements showing 78% erasure at 2.25 camera px/module delivering 4.0 KB/s). The design trades some pixel safety for higher tile count and throughput; the table illustrates the *relationship* between M, screen px/module, and camera px/module, not the exact design parameters.\n\n**Two independent approaches; do not compose them.** There are two ways to increase M:\n\n1. **Sender-side:** Shape the code region to match the receiver's orientation (540×960 portrait region for portrait receiver). This is the **primary, always-on path** — the sender uses this region by default.\n2. **Receiver-side:** Physically rotate the receiver device (landscape orientation for landscape receiver). This gives M = 2.78 × sender's M.\n\n**Do not combine these approaches.** A sender-side portrait region (M=2.0) combined with a receiver-side landscape orientation would give M ≈ 5.6, achieving ~11 camera px/module at 2 screen px/module — 3× more than needed, and at half the tiles that geometry could carry. Use exactly one approach: either the sender-side portrait region (default) OR the receiver-side landscape rotation (optional), not both.\n\n**Receiver-side landscape is a free bonus, not a requirement.** Physically holding the receiver in landscape puts the screen's long axis on the camera's long axis — 1.78× more magnification for free. It is worth *offering* to a user willing to turn the phone. But the app MUST NOT depend on the user doing so: the sender-side portrait region (above) is the primary, always-on path, and landscape is strictly an optional upgrade for extra margin on top of it.\n\n**Orientation handling.** The sender does not configure the receiver's OS orientation — that is impossible without a back-channel. Instead, the sender shapes its code region for the expected receiver orientation (portrait by default), and the receiver's UI coaches the user to match that orientation (§11, `E-ORIENTATION`). For the optional landscape bonus, the receiver's surface coaches the user to turn the device sideways; a physical turn is required because sensor mapping follows the device body, not the UI.\n\n### 6.4 Receiver pipeline\n\n```\ngetUserMedia ──► exposureCompensation:min (D14) ──► measure real fps (rVFC, ~1 s)\n      │\n      └──► requestVideoFrameCallback ──► MediaStreamTrackProcessor*\n                                                │\n                              ROI crop (conditional — see §6.4)\n                                                │\n                              ┌─────────────────┴──── Worker pool ────┐\n                              ▼                                       ▼\n                      zxing readBarcodes                     [Stage 2: split\n                      (all symbols, .bytes)                   R/G/B, stretch, ×3]\n                              │\n                    header parse ──► fcrc ──► streamId lock ──► route by blockIndex\n                              │                                        │\n                     beacon? ──┴──► learn size/blocks/K/hash    payload ──► GE decoder\n                                    (gates everything)\n                                                        rank == K ──► write to OPFS\n                                                                  ──► mark decode bitmap\n                                                                  ──► verify hash (if manifest present)\n                                                                  ──► mark verified bitmap\n                                                                              │\n                                            all blocks present & manifest decoded ──► verify all blocks\n                                                                  ──► [decompress] ──► compute whole-file hash ──► compare with beacon ──► save (or E-FILE-HASH if mismatch)\n```\n\n\\* `MediaStreamTrackProcessor` is **Chromium-only**; `requestVideoFrameCallback` +\n`drawImage` is the universal fallback and MUST be implemented (§6.5).\n\n**Block-layer working set: 264.0 KB** — 72.0 KB matrix + 192.0 KB block — flat regardless\nof file size. This is *not* the whole-receiver figure; see I6a/I6b in §5. The **total peak\nworking set is 528.0 KB** when including the manifest GE context (72.0 KB matrix + 192.0 KB block)\nand recover()'s second K*L array, still well under I6a's 1 MB limit (0.52×).\n\nThree rules that are cheap to implement and expensive to omit:\n\n- **Measure fps, never trust it.** `getSettings()` reports 30/60 while the camera\n  delivers 15.\n- **Crop to ROI before decoding — but the 9× is conditional.** Measured 8.6× (56.9 → 6.6 ms)\n  *when the code occupies part of the frame*. Once the grid fills the frame — which is what\n  you want for camera px/module — **the ROI is the frame and the win evaporates** (69 ms).\n  ROI is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput optimisation at the\n  right distance. **Except at high capture resolution**, where a tight quad-crop is what keeps\n  camera px/module high *and* pixel count bounded at once — there it is load-bearing, and must\n  be far tighter than the spike's 35%-margin version.\n- **Select capture resolution deliberately — it is a first-class tunable.** Measured knee:\n  720p → 100% erasure (1.5 camera px/module, nothing decodes); 1080p → best goodput; 4K →\n  zero empty frames but 194 ms decode and 1.1 fps, net *worse*. Decode is O(pixels), so more\n  resolution is not free. `getUserMedia` defaults are **not** adequate: a Pixel 6 defaults to\n  1080 on the *short* edge.\n- **Shape the code region to the camera, not the screen (sender-side, §6.3.2).**\n- **Never offer a torch button.** It measured a 3.6× fps gain, which makes it tempting,\n  but an LED on a glossy screen creates a specular hotspot that destroys a region of the\n  frame. `exposureCompensation` gets the same mechanism without glare.\n\n### 6.5 Module layout and dependency pins\n\nCommitted in Phase 0 so \"where does this go?\" is not re-litigated eight phases running.\nNote the layer boundaries of §6.1 and the thread boundaries of §6.2 are **not** the same,\nso the tree separates them explicitly.\n\n```\nsrc/\n  core/                 # At 2.7 KB per 4 GB for the bitmaps this is nearly free; the manifest adds\n921\t87 KB for a 4 GB file (21,845 blocks × 4-byte hashes). **The manifest MUST be persisted** — without it,\n922\tresume cannot re-verify blocks, and a reload during the ~12 minute manifest acquisition window would lose\n923\tall received blocks.\n924\t\n925\tThe sender is stateless across restarts by construction (D24) **when compression is disabled** —\n926\tit needs only the same file and the same `streamId` (§7.4). **With compression enabled, resume is\n927\tNOT supported** — see `docs/notes/bf-17s0-resume-compression-conflict.md` for the full analysis,\n928\t`docs/notes/bf-3k90-compression-resume-solution-evaluation.md` for the solution evaluation,\n929\tand `notes/bf-2w1a.md` for validation and test coverage.\n930\tThe short version: `CompressionStream` offers no determinism guarantee, so re-compression after\n931\tstaging is reaped (E11) would produce different blocks and silently corrupt the receiver's state.\n932\tThe beacon carries a `ResumeDisabled` flag (beacon `flags` field) when compression is on;\n933\tthe receiver uses this flag to suppress resume UI and prevent persisting resume tokens.\n934\tThis preserves the T4 privacy requirement (staging is still wiped on startup) while preventing\n935\tsilent corruption.\n936\t\n937\t**On resume the receiver MUST re-verify block hashes** rather than trusting the bitmap, in\n938\tcase OPFS was corrupted or the file was touched externally. This requires the manifest to be\n939\tpersisted alongside the bitmap.\n940\t\n941\t**Pre-manifest reload behavior:** If the receiver is reloaded before the manifest arrives\n942\t(e.g., during the ~12 minute acquisition window for a 4 GB file at the beacon's ~2 s cadence),\n943\tthe persisted bitmap preserves which blocks were decoded, and the written blocks remain in OPFS.\n944\tThe `writtenBlocks` bitmap is reset on resume, and blocks are re-verified once the manifest arrives.\n945\tThis prevents losing all received blocks during the manifest acquisition window.\n946\t\n947\t### 8.4 Storage limits\n948\t\n949\t| Platform | Practical quota |\n950\t|---|---|\n951\t| Chrome / Edge desktop | ~60% of free disk — multi-GB fine |\n952\t| Firefox | ~10% of disk (capped ~10 GB) |\n953\t| **Safari / iOS** | **~1 GB** before prompting; expandable but user-gated |\n954\t\n955\t**Multi-GB reception is a desktop-Chromium story.** The app MUST query\n956\t`navigator.storage.estimate()` up front and refuse clearly (§13.1) rather than failing at\n957\thour 9. Edge case catalog\n987\t\n988\t| # | Case | Resolution |\n989\t|---|---|---|\n990\t| E1 | **Zero-byte file** | Reject at selection with `E-ZERO-BYTE-FILE`. `K = 0` is undefined. |\n991\t| E2 | **File smaller than one fragment** (< 256 B) | Pad to one fragment; `K = 1`; the fountain code degenerates to repetition, which is correct. Research specifies a `K < 8` guard — adopt it: below 8 fragments, send plain repetition, no LT. **Repetition is derived per-block** (not signalled): both encoder and decoder derive `repetition = (k < MIN_LT_K)` from the block's K using the shared per-block derivation E3a already mandates. A session-wide flag would force repetition on all 21,845 blocks or none; per-block derivation allows the last block (K=1-7) to use repetition while all other blocks (K=768) use LT. |\n992\t| E3a | **The last block is short** — its K is `ceil(lastLen / L)`, not 768. Both sides derive K per block, and D7's PRNG is seeded with it. A mismatch produces wrong index sets, so the block never decodes and nothing says why. | Derive per-block K from `(blockIndex, blockSize, payloadLen)` in **one shared function** used by both encoder and decoder; conformance vector covers the last block explicitly. The beacon's `payloadLen` field (§7.2) is critical — without it, the receiver cannot compute the last block's actual length (`lastLen = payloadLen − (blockCount − 1) × blockSize`), leading to PRNG index mismatch and silent decode failure. |\n993\t| E3b | **`blockCount == 1`** | Normal path; no special case, but tested explicitly since off-by-one in block iteration is likely. |\n994\t| E4 | **Incompressible input where deflate expands it** | D8 samples first; if the sample ratio > 0.92, skip compression. If compression still expands, discard the staging file and send raw. Emit `E-INCOMPRESSIBLE-EXPANDS` as a warning. |\n995\t| E5 | **Source file changes mid-transfer** | A 10-hour read of a live `File` handle is the *normal* case. Re-check `file.size` and `lastModified` before each block read; on mismatch abort with `E-SOURCE-CHANGED`. Emitting blocks from two versions would produce a file that passes per-block hashes and fails the whole-file hash after hours. |\n996\t| E6 | **Duplicate packet arrives** | GE reduces it to a zero row; contributes nothing, costs one reduction. No special handling. |\n997\t| E7 | **Two senders in frame** | `streamId` lock (A9); packets from the unlocked stream are discarded and surfaced as `E-FOREIGN-STREAM`. |\n998\t| E8 | **Tab backgrounded on the sender** | `rAF` stops in a background tab, so a 10-hour transfer silently halts. Wake Lock does **not** cover this. Detect via `visibilitychange` and warn loudly; the transfer is paused, not failed. |\n999\t| E9 | **Camera permission revoked mid-run** | Pause, preserve the bitmap, prompt for re-grant. Never discard collected blocks. |\n1000\t| E10 | **OPFS quota exhausted mid-transfer** | Stop, keep completed blocks, export a partial file plus a manifest of what is missing. Never silently truncate. **The kept partial artefact follows T4b's deletion lifecycle** — warn the user before keeping it, provide a delete control, and reap on startup. |\n1001\t| E11 | **Abandoned staging file** | Sender-side staging keyed by `streamId`; on startup, reap staging files with no active session. Emit `E-BLOCK-HASH`. Block may already be written to OPFS but is never surfaced until verified (I9). This is the CRC-8 false-accept path (§7.1) and MUST be implemented — at GB scale a silent re-do costs hours. |\n1003\t| E13 | **Whole-file hash fails after all blocks pass** | Indicates E5 or a block-hash collision. Report `E-FILE-HASH`; keep the output and label it unverified rather than deleting hours of work. |\n1004\t| E14 | **Filename with path separators or control bytes** | Sanitise on export (§12, T2). Never write an attacker-chosen path. |\n1005\t| E15 | **Decompression fails at the end** | All blocks verified (per-block hashes passed) but the gzip stream is invalid → `E-DECOMPRESS`. Keep the compressed artefact so nothing is lost, but note that **the whole-file hash cannot be evaluated** — it requires successful decompression to compute. The kept artefact follows T4b's deletion lifecycle: warn the user before keeping it (explicitly noting it is **unverified**), provide a delete control, and reap on startup. The compressed artefact is received data that passed per-block verification but failed the final format conversion (decompression); it cannot be surfaced to the user as the original file. |\n1006\t| E16 | **Worker crash mid-block** | Restart the worker, discard the active block only, keep the bitmap. Emit `E-WORKER-CRASH`. |\n1007\t| E17a | **Sender-side thermal throttling** | Observed: the bench laptop decayed 6.7 → 2.4 fps over two minutes. See `docs/notes/bf-3mnt-thermal-throttling-discrimination.md` for discrimination logic. The receiver MUST NOT duty-cycle in response to sender-side throttling — doing so would multiply transfer time without addressing the root cause. |\n1008\t| E17b | **Receiver-side thermal throttling** | Observed at **70 °C / throttling threshold within 20–30 minutes**.
